property_summary: For every deployer address, the deployed contract's owner() getter must return the deployer address (the Ownable owner), but the mutant returns address(0) breaking this for many deployers.
For any deployer address D, the contract's owner() getter returns D (the deployer); the mutant returns address(0) for some deployers, violating this.

For any caller address A used to call owner() on C, the deployed correct contract returns the stored owner value equal to the internal _owner (which is set to the deployer in constructor and remains non-zero after construction), whereas the mutant returns address(0) for some inputs; thus the property: calling owner() never returns address(0) for any nonzero deployer-derived owner in the reference, but the mutant can return address(0).

For any fuzzed deployer address used by the constructor (the contract is deployed in setUp with the test contract as deployer), the reference contract's owner() always returns the non-zero owner address (the stored owner), whereas the mutant's owner() may return address(0); we assert owner() != address(0) always holds on the reference, which the mutant breaks for some inputs.

For every fuzzed caller address A, calling owner() on the correct contract returns a non-zero address (the stored owner), whereas the mutant returns address(0) breaking that rule for some inputs; thus assert owner() != address(0) always holds on the reference but not on the mutant.

For any caller address, the real contract's owner() always returns the stored owner (the deployer) — i.e., owner() != caller for at least some callers — while the mutant incorrectly returns msg.sender causing owner() == caller for callers other than the true owner.

For every caller address x, the reference contract's owner() returns the fixed deployer address (the stored owner) — it is independent of msg.sender — while the mutant returns msg.sender causing owner() to equal the caller for some callers (i.e., owner() == caller for callers other than the deployer), so there exists inputs where returned value differs.

For any caller address, the reference contract's owner() always returns the stored deployer-owner (independent of msg.sender); the mutant returns msg.sender causing owner() to equal the caller for some callers — so the property is that owner() equals the deployer for every caller, which the bug violates for callers other than the deployer.

For any caller address, calling owner() on the correct contract always returns the fixed deployer-owner address (the stored owner); the mutant may instead return the caller's address (msg.sender), so there exist callers for which owner() differs from the stored deployer-owner.

For every caller address, calling owner() on the reference contract returns the same address irrespective of who calls (the stored owner set in constructor); the mutant that returns msg.sender violates this by making owner() vary with the caller, so there exist callers for which owner() differs from the stored owner.

For every deployment the contract's owner() returns the deployer address (msg.sender during construction); the mutant returning tx.origin can differ when deployment is done by a contract (tx.origin != deployer), so the mutant violates the rule for some deployer contract-created instances.

For any deployer EOA or contract that calls C.owner(), the canonical contract's owner() always equals msg.sender while the mutant that returns tx.origin will differ whenever the call is made via a contract (msg.sender != tx.origin), so invoking owner() through an intermediate caller contract yields different return values in the mutant but not in the reference.

For any caller address X, calling c.owner() directly (msg.sender == X) returns X in the reference contract (owner() == msg.sender), whereas the mutant that returns tx.origin can return a different value when owner() is invoked through an intermediate contract (tx.origin != msg.sender), so calling owner() via an intermediary contract will produce mismatched results in the mutant but not in the reference.

For every caller address A (fuzzed), calling c.owner() directly returns the same owner value as msg.sender would (the reference returns the deployer/owner address when called by that caller), whereas the mutant that returns tx.origin can produce a different value when the call is made via a contract call chain where tx.origin differs from msg.sender; therefore the reference preserves equality owner() == msg.sender for direct calls, while the mutant can break equality when owner() is invoked via an intermediate contract that forwards the call.

For any caller address A, calling c.owner() directly from A returns the contract's stored owner (msg.sender during construction) as reported by the reference (owner() == the deployer/owner), but the mutant that returns tx.origin will sometimes differ when owner() is invoked via an intermediate contract whose tx.origin is different from the immediate msg.sender; specifically, the reference's owner() always equals the stored owner value when read directly, whereas the mutant can return tx.origin which can differ — the test calls owner() directly from arbitrary EOAs to show the reference's owner equals the deployer (address(this) used at construction) for all inputs, but the mutant will be distinguishable when the fuzzer provides a different caller that makes the call via a forwarding contract (the forwarded call reveals the tx.origin-vs-msg.sender mismatch).

For any deployer address, the contract's owner() getter must return the deployer (the externally-owned account that constructed the contract); the mutant that returns address(this) breaks this by returning the contract address instead for some deployers.

For every deployer address X, C.owner() returns the deployer (msg.sender at construction); the mutant that hardcodes owner() to return address(this) causes owner() to equal the contract address for some deployers, violating that rule.

For every deployer address D, calling owner() on the deployed contract returns the deployer D; the mutant that makes owner() return address(this) will for some deployers return the contract address instead, violating this property.

For every deployer address, the contract's owner() getter returns the externally-owned account that constructed the contract (the deployer); the mutant that returns address(this) will instead return the contract address for some deployers, violating this rule.

For every address caller A that calls the constructor via new C(A) (deployer), the reference contract's owner() returns that deployer address, whereas the mutant that returns address(this) will for some deployers return the contract's own address instead — so owner() should never equal address(c) for any deployer that is an EOA; the mutant violates this when the deployer is not the contract itself.

For any non-zero caller who is the owner and any address newOwner, the reference contract reverts (fails) when attempting transferOwnership(address(0)) while allowing non-zero addresses; the mutant removes the zero-address check so it will succeed for newOwner == address(0).

For any caller that is the current owner and any candidate newOwner address, the reference contract rejects setting the zero address as owner (transferOwnership(address(0)) reverts) while the mutant allows it; i.e. transferOwnership(newOwner) should revert iff newOwner == address(0).

For any caller who is the current owner and any candidate newOwner address, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) on the reference contract reverts if and only if newOwner == address(0); the mutant removed the zero-address check so it allows transferOwnership(address(0)), violating that rule.

For any candidate newOwner address, the reference contract reverts when the owner tries to transferOwnership to the zero address while succeeding for non-zero addresses; the mutant removes the zero-address check so it will succeed for newOwner == address(0), violating this rule.

For any address newOwner and when called by the current owner, transferOwnership(newOwner) on the reference contract reverts if and only if newOwner is the zero address; the mutant removes the zero-address require and thus allows transferOwnership(address(0)), changing the resulting owner — so the property is that transferOwnership(address(0)) must revert (reference) while mutant may succeed.

For any caller that is the current owner, calling transferOwnership with any non-zero address succeeds (owner becomes that address); the mutant wrongly only allows setting owner to the zero address, so transferring to a non-zero address will fail there for some inputs.

For any newOwner address, the correct contract allows the current owner to transfer ownership to any non-zero address (call succeeds and owner becomes newOwner); the mutant instead only permits transferring ownership to the zero address, causing calls with non-zero newOwner to revert or fail for some inputs.

For any fuzzed candidate newOwner address, when the current owner calls transferOwnership(newOwner) the reference C allows the call to succeed exactly when newOwner is any address (including non-zero) — specifically, calling transferOwnership with newOwner == address(0) is allowed by reference only if owner calls renounceOwnership, whereas calling transferOwnership with any non-zero newOwner should succeed on the reference but will fail on the mutant that requires newOwner == address(0); thus there exists fuzzed newOwner inputs (non-zero addresses) for which the mutant rejects the call while the reference accepts it.

For any address newOwner and when called by the current owner, transferOwnership(newOwner) completes successfully on the reference and results in owner() == newOwner; the mutant instead only allows newOwner == address(0), so there exist fuzzed non-zero addresses for which the mutant call fails (or yields a different owner).

For any address newOwner and when called by the contract owner, transferOwnership(newOwner) on the reference C succeeds (call does not revert) and sets owner() == newOwner; the mutant instead requires newOwner == address(0) causing calls with many fuzzed non-zero newOwner inputs to fail — so the reference never reverts for owner-called transferOwnership while the mutant sometimes does.

For any caller address X and newOwner address Y, only the current owner can successfully call transferOwnership(Y) on the reference contract (so transferOwnership succeeds when called by owner and updates owner to Y); the mutant requiring caller == address(0) breaks this by making transferOwnership fail for the real owner (and succeed only if the zero address could call), so there exist inputs where behavior differs.

For any caller address A and target newOwner N, in the reference contract transferOwnership called by the current owner succeeds (updates owner to N); the mutant replaces onlyOwner to require caller == address(0), so transferOwnership called by the real owner will revert for some inputs, breaking that property.

For any caller address addr and any target newOwner, when the current owner calls transferOwnership(newOwner) the call succeeds and owner() becomes newOwner in the correct contract; the mutant instead only allows the zero address to act as owner so a transferOwnership call by the real owner can revert or fail to update owner(), violating this rule for some inputs.

For any caller address 'caller' and any target 'newOwner', in the correct contract a transferOwnership(newOwner) call made by the current owner succeeds (owner() becomes newOwner); the mutant changes onlyOwner to require caller == address(0) so a transferOwnership call by the real owner may revert or fail to change owner(), violating this rule for some fuzzed inputs.

For any candidate newOwner, when the current owner calls transferOwnership(newOwner) on the correct contract it succeeds (call does not revert) and after the call owner() equals newOwner; the mutant requiring onlyOwner to accept only address(0) causes the transferOwnership call by the real owner to revert for some fuzzed newOwner inputs, breaking this rule.

For all calls, the reference contract's name() returns the token's stored name string (the constructor-provided _name), whereas the mutant returns a hard-coded different literal, so name() must equal "DCF Token" for all inputs on the reference but will differ for some inputs on the mutant.

For any input the contract's public name() must return the stored token name set in the constructor ("DCF Token"); the mutant returns a different fixed literal, so for some inputs name() will not equal the stored name.

For every (fuzzed) caller address, calling the public getter name() on the correct contract returns the constructor-set token name string "DCF Token" (the stored _name), whereas the mutant returns a different literal so some caller will observe a different returned string; the test asserts that name() equals the expected stored name for all inputs by calling name() (via try/catch) and checking equality.

For any caller address, the reference contract's public name() call always returns the constructor-set token name "DCF Token"; the mutant returns a different fixed literal for some callers, so there exists an input where the returned string differs.

For every caller address, the reference contract's name() returns the constructor-initialized token name string "DCF Token"; the mutant returns a different fixed literal, so there exist caller addresses for which the observed returned string differs, violating this invariant.

For any call to symbol(), the reference contract always returns the stored _symbol string (the token's symbol), whereas the mutant returns a different hard-coded string for some inputs (i.e., callers), so the returned string must equal the deployed token's symbol in the reference but can differ in the mutant.

For any caller address, the deployed reference contract's symbol() returns the token's stored symbol string ("DCF"), whereas the mutant returns a different hard-coded string for some callers, so symbol() must equal the deployed token's stored symbol for all callers (the mutant can break this by returning "DCT").

For any caller, the reference contract's symbol() returns the token's stored symbol string ("DCF"); the mutant returns a different hard-coded string ("DCT") for some inputs, so the returned string must equal the deployed token's actual symbol in the reference but can differ in the mutant.

For every caller address, the reference contract's symbol() returns the token's stored symbol string (which equals c.name()'s symbol stored at construction), whereas the mutant returns a different hard-coded string for some callers; thus for all addresses symbol() should equal the reference symbol value, and the mutant will produce a differing return for some input address.

For every caller address, the reference contract returns the stored token symbol string (the value set at construction) from symbol(); the mutant returns a different hard-coded string for some callers, so asserting that c.symbol() equals c.name() (both view calls) holds for all inputs on the reference but is violated by the mutant for some fuzzed caller address.

For every call, the correct contract's symbol() returns the stored non-empty token symbol string, while the mutant may return an empty string for some inputs, so symbol() must be non-empty for all calls on the reference but is empty on the mutant for some call.

For any caller address, the reference contract's symbol() returns a non-empty string, whereas the mutant returns an empty string for some callers; thus symbol() != "" always holds on the reference but can be false on the mutant.
For any caller address, C.symbol() returns a non-empty string (the stored token symbol); the mutant returns an empty string for some calls, violating this invariant.
For all callers, C.symbol() returns a non-empty string (the stored token symbol); the mutant returns an empty string for some calls, breaking this invariant.

For every caller address, the reference contract's symbol() returns a non-empty string; the mutant returns an empty string for some calls, so the property 'symbol() != "" for any caller' holds for the reference but is violated by the mutant.

For any call to symbol(), the reference contract always returns its stored _symbol value (different from name()); the mutant that returns name() will therefore sometimes return a different string when name() != _symbol.

For every input, the deployed correct contract returns symbol() equal to its stored symbol (i.e., equal to ERC20 symbol getter), which differs from name() in the mutant for some inputs where name() != symbol(); the test fuzzes an input to detect when name() != symbol() and asserts symbol() == symbol() (via comparing symbol() to itself in reference) while mutant returns name() causing mismatch with expected stored symbol read via name() (fuzzer finds differing names), so the mutant fails.

For any deployment, C.symbol() always returns the token's stored symbol string; the mutant returns name() instead, so when name() != symbol() the mutant yields a different return value and the property is violated.

For any fuzzed input string s (used to compare name() vs symbol()), the deployed correct contract C always returns a symbol() equal to its stored symbol (which is different from name()), so symbol() == c.symbol() holds for all inputs; the mutant that returns name() will sometimes make symbol() != name(), violating the equality when the fuzzer picks a distinguishing check comparing symbol() to name().

For every deployment and any (fuzzed) caller address, C.symbol() returns the token's stored symbol string (different from name()); the mutant returns name() instead, so comparing symbol() to name() will always hold for the reference but fail for the mutant whenever name() != symbol().

For every call, the reference contract C.decimals() always returns 18 (ERC20 standard decimals), while the mutant returns 8 for some inputs — therefore the universal property is that decimals() == 18 for all calls; the bug breaks this by returning 8 for the same call.

For any caller address input, the reference contract always returns 18 from decimals(); the mutant returns a different value (8) for some caller addresses, so there exists an input where decimals() != 18.
